items.stem: Which of the following best describes "optionality (participation)"?
options: The ability to change one level of the schema without having to change the levels above it
A diagram showing the entities in a system, their attributes and the relationships and cardinalities between them
Automatic checking by a program or DBMS that input data is sensible and obeys defined rules before it is accepted
Whether an entity instance must take part in a relationship (mandatory) or may not (optional)
items.answer: Whether an entity instance must take part in a relationship (mandatory) or may not (optional)
items.markingKey: D. "optionality (participation)" is whether an entity instance must take part in a relationship (mandatory) or may not (optional).

items.stem: A student claims that in a one-to-many relationship between Customer and Order, the OrderID should be stored in the Customer table. Identify the error in this claim and correct it.
items.answer: The foreign key goes on the many side: CustomerID is stored in Order. Storing OrderIDs in Customer would need a list of values in one field.
items.markingKey: The foreign key goes on the many side: CustomerID is stored in Order. Storing OrderIDs in Customer would need a list of values in one field. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem: Distinguish between a mandatory relationship and an optional relationship.
items.answer: In a mandatory relationship every instance must participate (each Order must have a Customer); in an optional one an instance may have no related record (a Customer may have no Orders yet).
items.markingKey: In a mandatory relationship every instance must participate (each Order must have a Customer); in an optional one an instance may have no related record (a Customer may have no Orders yet). One mark for a correct account of each side; further marks for making the difference explicit (not two separate definitions).

items.stem: The following business rules apply to a secondary school in Singapore. Students take several courses and each course is taken by many students. For each relationship, state its cardinality and describe how it would be implemented in a relational database.
items.answer: Student–Course: many-to-many (M:N) – create a link table StudentCourse containing StudentID and CourseID as foreign keys forming a composite primary key
items.markingKey: Student–Course: many-to-many (M:N) – create a link table StudentCourse containing StudentID and CourseID as foreign keys forming a composite primary key. 1 mark per correct cardinality, 1 mark per correct implementation.

items.stem:
(a) Outline the meaning of the term "link (junction) table". [2]
(b) Explain the difference between a logical ERD and a conceptual ERD. [2]
(c) The following business rules apply to an airline based in Dubai. A passenger takes many flights and a flight carries many passengers. Crew members work on many flights and each flight has several crew. For each relationship, state its cardinality and describe how it would be implemented in a relational database. [4]
items.answer: (a) A table that resolves a many-to-many relationship into two one-to-many relationships by holding the keys of both entities (b) A conceptual ERD shows entities and relationships only, possibly with M:N; a logical ERD adds attributes, keys and resolves M:N relationships ready for tables. (c) Passenger–Flight: many-to-many (M:N) – create a link table PassengerFlight containing PassengerID and FlightID as foreign keys forming a composite primary key; CrewMember–Flight: many-to-many (M:N) – create a link table CrewMemberFlight containing CrewMemberID and FlightID as foreign keys forming a composite primary key
items.markingKey: (a) [2 marks] 1 mark for the core idea: a table that resolves a many-to-many relationship into two one-to-many relationships by holding the keys of both entities. Award full marks only if the defining feature is clear; a vague example alone scores 0. (b) [2 marks] A conceptual ERD shows entities and relationships only, possibly with M:N; a logical ERD adds attributes, keys and resolves M:N relationships ready for tables. One mark for a correct account of each side; further marks for making the difference explicit (not two separate definitions). (c) [4 marks] Passenger–Flight: many-to-many (M:N) – create a link table PassengerFlight containing PassengerID and FlightID as foreign keys forming a composite primary key; CrewMember–Flight: many-to-many (M:N) – create a link table CrewMemberFlight containing CrewMemberID and FlightID as foreign keys forming a composite primary key. 1 mark per correct cardinality, 1 mark per correct implementation.

items.stem: A designer for a secondary school in Singapore records these rules. Each student is allocated one locker and each locker is allocated to one student. A teacher teaches many classes; each class has one teacher. A department employs many teachers; each teacher belongs to one department. A student may join many clubs and each club has many students. Students take several courses and each course is taken by many students. Determine the minimum number of tables needed in a normalised relational implementation, naming each table.
items.answer: 9 tables: Student, Locker, Teacher, Class, Department, Club, Course plus link table(s) StudentClub, StudentCourse.
items.markingKey: One table per entity (7) (M1) plus one link table for each many-to-many relationship (2) (M1); 9 tables: Student, Locker, Teacher, Class, Department, Club, Course plus link table(s) StudentClub, StudentCourse. (A1).

items.stem: A music-streaming service in Seoul stores Artists, Albums, Tracks and Playlists. An artist releases many albums; an album has many tracks; a track can appear on many playlists and a playlist contains many tracks; each playlist is created by one user and a user can create many playlists. Describe the ERD (entities, relationships and cardinalities) and list the tables with their primary and foreign keys.
items.answer: Entities: Artist, Album, Track, Playlist, User, PlaylistTrack (link). Artist 1:M Album; Album 1:M Track; User 1:M Playlist; Track M:N Playlist resolved by PlaylistTrack. Tables: Artist(ArtistID PK, Name), Album(AlbumID PK, Title, ArtistID FK), Track(TrackID PK, Title, Duration, AlbumID FK), User(UserID PK, Name), Playlist(PlaylistID PK, Name, UserID FK), PlaylistTrack(PlaylistID FK, TrackID FK, Position; PK (PlaylistID, TrackID)).
items.markingKey: Entities: Artist, Album, Track, Playlist, User, PlaylistTrack (link). Artist 1:M Album; Album 1:M Track; User 1:M Playlist; Track M:N Playlist resolved by PlaylistTrack. Tables: Artist(ArtistID PK, Name), Album(AlbumID PK, Title, ArtistID FK), Track(TrackID PK, Title, Duration, AlbumID FK), User(UserID PK, Name), Playlist(PlaylistID PK, Name, UserID FK), PlaylistTrack(PlaylistID FK, TrackID FK, Position; PK (PlaylistID, TrackID)).

items.stem:
Case study context: Alpine Rescue in Vienna logs mountain incidents with GPS coordinates in a spatial database, predicts avalanche risk from weather features and coordinates teams with an OOP dispatch system.
(a) Explain the difference between an entity and an attribute. Refer to Alpine Rescue in Vienna in your answer. [2]
(b) Evaluate the claim that an ERD is unnecessary for a small database with only three tables. Refer to Alpine Rescue in Vienna in your answer. [4]
items.answer: (a) An entity is an object about which data is stored (e.g. Patient), becoming a table; an attribute is a property of that entity (e.g. DateOfBirth), becoming a field. (b) A quick ERD is still worthwhile because it is cheap and prevents structural errors that are costly to fix after data is loaded.
items.markingKey: (a) [2 marks] An entity is an object about which data is stored (e.g. Patient), becoming a table; an attribute is a property of that entity (e.g. DateOfBirth), becoming a field. One mark for a correct account of each side; further marks for making the difference explicit (not two separate definitions). (b) [4 marks] Arguments for: for very small systems the relationships may be obvious; saves design time. Arguments against: even small designs can contain M:N relationships or wrong cardinalities; documentation helps future maintenance and communication with the client; small systems often grow. Supported judgement: A quick ERD is still worthwhile because it is cheap and prevents structural errors that are costly to fix after data is loaded. Markbands: top band: well-balanced discussion with accurate, specific technical detail applied to the context and a justified conclusion; middle band: some balance and correct terminology, conclusion only partly supported; bottom band: descriptive, largely one-sided, little technical detail or application. Credit is given only for points applied to the stated organisation (not generic answers).

items.stem: Define the term "link (junction) table".
items.answer: A table that resolves a many-to-many relationship into two one-to-many relationships by holding the keys of both entities
items.markingKey: 1 mark for the core idea: a table that resolves a many-to-many relationship into two one-to-many relationships by holding the keys of both entities. Award full marks only if the defining feature is clear; a vague example alone scores 0.

items.stem: Explain why the foreign key is placed on the "many" side of a one-to-many relationship.
items.answer: Each record on the many side relates to exactly one record on the one side, so it can store a single foreign key value; placing it on the one side would need a list of values.
items.markingKey: Award marks for: Each record on the many side relates to exactly one record on the one side, so it can store a single foreign key value; placing it on the one side would need a list of values. (2 marks: one for each linked point in the chain of reasoning; no marks for assertion without explanation.)

items.stem:
Assertion (A): A link table is needed to implement a many-to-many relationship.
Reason (R): A field in a relational table must contain a single atomic value.
Which option is correct?
options: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true but R is false.
A is false but R is true.
items.answer: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
items.markingKey: A. Both true; atomic fields are why a link table is needed.

items.stem: A designer for a secondary school in Singapore records these rules. Each student is allocated one locker and each locker is allocated to one student. A teacher teaches many classes; each class has one teacher. Students take several courses and each course is taken by many students. Determine the minimum number of tables needed in a normalised relational implementation, naming each table.
items.answer: 6 tables: Student, Locker, Teacher, Class, Course plus link table(s) StudentCourse.
items.markingKey: One table per entity (5) (M1) plus one link table for each many-to-many relationship (1) (M1); 6 tables: Student, Locker, Teacher, Class, Course plus link table(s) StudentCourse. (A1).

items.stem: The following business rules apply to a hospital in Nairobi. A doctor treats many patients and a patient can be treated by several doctors. A ward holds many patients; an admitted patient is in one ward. For each relationship, state its cardinality and describe how it would be implemented in a relational database.
items.answer: Doctor–Patient: many-to-many (M:N) – create a link table DoctorPatient containing DoctorID and PatientID as foreign keys forming a composite primary key; Ward–Patient: one-to-many (1:M) – put the primary key of Ward as a foreign key in Patient
items.markingKey: Doctor–Patient: many-to-many (M:N) – create a link table DoctorPatient containing DoctorID and PatientID as foreign keys forming a composite primary key; Ward–Patient: one-to-many (1:M) – put the primary key of Ward as a foreign key in Patient. 1 mark per correct cardinality, 1 mark per correct implementation.

items.stem: Analyse one strength and one limitation of the view that an ERD is unnecessary for a small database with only three tables.
items.answer: A quick ERD is still worthwhile because it is cheap and prevents structural errors that are costly to fix after data is loaded.
items.markingKey: Arguments for: for very small systems the relationships may be obvious; saves design time. Arguments against: even small designs can contain M:N relationships or wrong cardinalities; documentation helps future maintenance and communication with the client; small systems often grow. Supported judgement: A quick ERD is still worthwhile because it is cheap and prevents structural errors that are costly to fix after data is loaded.

items.stem: Which term matches this description: "The process of organising tables to reduce data redundancy and remove insert, update and delete anomalies"?
options: external schema (view)
normalisation
functional dependency
conceptual schema
items.answer: normalisation
items.markingKey: B. This is the definition of normalisation.

items.stem: "In 3NF there is no redundancy at all." Explain the flaw in this statement.
items.answer: 3NF removes redundancy caused by partial and transitive dependencies, but some redundancy (e.g. repeated foreign key values) is needed and some anomalies can remain until BCNF.
items.markingKey: 3NF removes redundancy caused by partial and transitive dependencies, but some redundancy (e.g. repeated foreign key values) is needed and some anomalies can remain until BCNF. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem: Explain why a fully normalised database may sometimes be deliberately denormalised.
items.answer: Highly normalised designs need many joins, which can slow read-heavy reporting; storing some redundant data (e.g. in a data warehouse) speeds up queries at the cost of extra storage and controlled redundancy.
items.markingKey: Award marks for: Highly normalised designs need many joins, which can slow read-heavy reporting; storing some redundant data (e.g. in a data warehouse) speeds up queries at the cost of extra storage and controlled redundancy. (3 marks: one for each linked point in the chain of reasoning; no marks for assertion without explanation.)

items.stem:
At an airline in Lima, an unnormalised table stores each flight with a repeating group of passengers:
F100: P81, P48, P48, P70
F101: P13, P28
F102: P63, P67, P41, P83
F103: P44
The table is converted to first normal form by giving each passenger its own row. State how many rows the 1NF table will contain and identify its primary key.
items.answer: 11 rows (one per flight-passenger pair); the primary key becomes the composite (FlightID, PassengerID).
items.markingKey: Count of repeating values 4 + 2 + 4 + 1 = 11 (A1); composite key (A1).

items.stem:
A table used by an online shop in Toronto is OrderLine(OrderID, ProductID, Quantity, UnitPrice, CustomerID, CustomerName) with the functional dependencies:
OrderID → CustomerID
ProductID → UnitPrice
CustomerID → CustomerName
OrderID, ProductID → Quantity
Identify the primary key and state the highest normal form the table is in, justifying your answer.
items.answer: Candidate key (OrderID, ProductID). Highest normal form: 1NF, because partial dependencies: CustomerID depends only on OrderID; CustomerName depends only on OrderID; UnitPrice depends only on ProductID and transitive dependencies: CustomerName depends on non-key CustomerID.
items.markingKey: Candidate key (OrderID, ProductID). Highest normal form: 1NF, because partial dependencies: CustomerID depends only on OrderID; CustomerName depends only on OrderID; UnitPrice depends only on ProductID and transitive dependencies: CustomerName depends on non-key CustomerID. 1 mark key; 1 mark normal form; 1-2 marks justification naming the specific dependencies.

items.stem:
(a) Outline the meaning of the term "third normal form (3NF)". [2]
(b) A school in Geneva stores Enrolment(StudentID, CourseID, StudentName, CourseTitle, TeacherName). The functional dependencies are:
StudentID → StudentName
CourseID → CourseTitle, TeacherName
Normalise the table to third normal form. Show each resulting table with its primary key. [5]
(c) A student claims that Normalisation always makes queries faster. Identify the error in this claim and correct it. [3]
items.answer: (a) A 2NF table in which no non-key attribute depends on another non-key attribute, so there are no transitive dependencies (b) 3 tables (key fields marked *): (StudentID*, StudentName); (CourseID*, CourseTitle, TeacherName); (StudentID*, CourseID*) (c) Normalisation reduces redundancy and anomalies but often requires more joins, which can make some queries slower.
items.markingKey: (a) [2 marks] 1 mark for the core idea: a 2NF table in which no non-key attribute depends on another non-key attribute, so there are no transitive dependencies. Award full marks only if the defining feature is clear; a vague example alone scores 0. (b) [5 marks] Key StudentID, CourseID identified (A1). Remove partial dependencies to reach 2NF (M1), remove transitive dependencies to reach 3NF (M1). Final: 3 tables (key fields marked *): (StudentID*, StudentName); (CourseID*, CourseTitle, TeacherName); (StudentID*, CourseID*) (A1 per correct table; foreign keys retained so the original data can be rejoined). (c) [3 marks] Normalisation reduces redundancy and anomalies but often requires more joins, which can make some queries slower. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem:
Case study context: Kente Market, an online craft marketplace in Accra, stores products as JSON documents, ranks listings with a neural network and processes orders through a queue-based service.
(a) Explain why normalisation reduces update anomalies. Refer to Kente Market in your answer. [3]
(b) Analyse one strength and one limitation of the view that Databases should always be normalised to third normal form. Refer to Kente Market in your answer. [3]
items.answer: (a) Each fact is stored once, in the table whose key determines it, so a change (e.g. a product price) is made in one row and cannot leave other copies inconsistent. (b) For transactional (OLTP) systems 3NF is the right default; for analytical or performance-critical read workloads controlled denormalisation can be justified.
items.markingKey: (a) [3 marks] Award marks for: Each fact is stored once, in the table whose key determines it, so a change (e.g. a product price) is made in one row and cannot leave other copies inconsistent. (one for each linked point in the chain of reasoning; no marks for assertion without explanation.) (b) [3 marks] Arguments for: removes redundancy and update/insert/delete anomalies; keeps data consistent and saves storage. Arguments against: more tables mean more joins, slowing read-heavy queries; data warehouses and analytics deliberately denormalise; design effort and complexity increase. Supported judgement: For transactional (OLTP) systems 3NF is the right default; for analytical or performance-critical read workloads controlled denormalisation can be justified. Credit is given only for points applied to the stated organisation (not generic answers).

items.stem: Outline the meaning of the term "partial dependency".
items.answer: A non-key attribute that depends on only part of a composite primary key
items.markingKey: 1 mark for the core idea: a non-key attribute that depends on only part of a composite primary key. Award full marks only if the defining feature is clear; a vague example alone scores 0.

items.stem:
Assertion (A): A table whose primary key is a single field cannot contain a partial dependency.
Reason (R): A partial dependency is a dependency on part of a composite key.
Which option is correct?
options: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true but R is false.
A is false but R is true.
items.answer: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
items.markingKey: A. Both true; the definition in R explains A.

items.stem: Explain the difference between 2NF and 3NF.
items.answer: 2NF removes partial dependencies on part of a composite key; 3NF additionally removes transitive dependencies between non-key attributes.
items.markingKey: 2NF removes partial dependencies on part of a composite key; 3NF additionally removes transitive dependencies between non-key attributes. One mark for a correct account of each side; further marks for making the difference explicit (not two separate definitions).

items.stem: State what is meant by the term "presence check".
items.answer: A validation rule that a required field is not left empty (NOT NULL)
items.markingKey: 1 mark for the core idea: a validation rule that a required field is not left empty (NOT NULL). Award full marks only if the defining feature is clear; a vague example alone scores 0.

items.stem: Freya writes: "A presence check makes sure that the data entered is correct." Explain why this is inaccurate.
items.answer: A presence check only ensures something has been entered; the value could still be wrong or invalid.
items.markingKey: A presence check only ensures something has been entered; the value could still be wrong or invalid. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem: Explain why boundary values must be included in test data for a range check.
items.answer: Off-by-one errors (using < instead of ≤) are common; testing values at and just beyond each limit shows whether the boundaries are accepted and rejected correctly.
items.markingKey: Award marks for: Off-by-one errors (using < instead of ≤) are common; testing values at and just beyond each limit shows whether the boundaries are accepted and rejected correctly. items.answer: 1: succeeds; 2: fails (CHECK constraint); 3: fails (CHECK constraint); 4: fails (CHECK constraint). Rows stored: 1.

items.stem:
(a) Outline the meaning of the term "range check". [2]
(b) Noah writes: "A presence check makes sure that the data entered is correct." Explain why this is inaccurate. [2]
(c) A program accepts the quantity ordered as a whole number from 1 to 50 inclusive. Construct a set of test data containing normal, boundary and erroneous values, with the expected outcome for each. [3]
items.answer: (a) A validation rule that a value lies between a lower and an upper limit (b) A presence check only ensures something has been entered; the value could still be wrong or invalid. (c) Normal: 24; boundary (extreme): 1 and 50; boundary rejected: 0 and 51; erroneous: e.g. "abc" or 24.5 (not an integer).

items.stem:
Case study context: Harvest Link, an agricultural cooperative near Nairobi, records crop sales in a database, uses sensors and a model to predict yields, and gives farmers an app that queues orders and caches prices in a hash table.
(a) Sana writes: "Constraints slow down a database so they should be removed." Explain why this is inaccurate. Refer to Harvest Link in your answer. [3]
(b) Give one argument for and one argument against the view that Validation in the application is sufficient; database constraints are unnecessary. Refer to Harvest Link in your answer. [3]
items.answer: (a) Constraints have a small cost but prevent invalid data entering; removing them risks inconsistent data, which is far more costly. (b) Both layers are needed: UI validation for usability and DBMS constraints as the final guarantee of integrity.
items.markingKey: (a) [3 marks] Constraints have a small cost but prevent invalid data entering; removing them risks inconsistent data, which is far more costly. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation. (b) [3 marks] Arguments for: application checks give immediate user feedback; fewer schema changes are needed. Arguments against: other applications, scripts and imports bypass application checks; constraints are enforced centrally and consistently; they document the rules in the schema. Supported judgement: Both layers are needed: UI validation for usability and DBMS constraints as the final guarantee of integrity. Credit is given only for points applied to the stated organisation (not generic answers).

update anomaly
entity

items.stem: Explain the difference between erroneous test data and normal test data.
items.answer: Normal data are typical valid values that should be accepted; erroneous data are invalid values (wrong type or out of range) that should be rejected.

entity
update anomaly

items.stem: Alessia writes: "The physical schema is designed first, because the hardware must be bought before anything else." Explain why this is inaccurate.
items.answer: Design proceeds from conceptual to logical to physical; hardware and storage choices depend on the agreed data requirements.

items.stem:
Assertion (A): The logical schema depends on the DBMS product chosen.
Reason (R): Data types such as VARCHAR(255) are DBMS-specific.
Which option is correct?
options: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true but R is false.
A is false but R is true.
items.answer: A is false but R is true.

items.stem: A designer for a hospital in Nairobi records these rules. A patient may be admitted many times; each admission is for one patient. A prescription can contain several drugs and a drug appears on many prescriptions. A ward holds many patients; an admitted patient is in one ward. items.stem:
(a) Define the term "second normal form (2NF)". [2]
(b) Explain the difference between a deletion anomaly and an insertion anomaly. [2]
(c) A table used by an online shop in Toronto is OrderLine(OrderID, ProductID, OrderDate, CustomerID, CustomerName) with the functional dependencies:
OrderID → CustomerID, OrderDate
CustomerID → CustomerName
Identify the primary key and state the highest normal form the table is in, justifying your answer. [3]
items.answer: (a) A 1NF table in which every non-key attribute depends on the whole primary key, so there are no partial dependencies (b) An insertion anomaly is being unable to add a fact without unrelated data (a new course with no students); a deletion anomaly is losing a fact unintentionally when deleting other data (deleting the last student removes the course). (c) Candidate key (OrderID, ProductID). Highest normal form: 1NF, because partial dependencies: CustomerID depends only on OrderID; CustomerName depends only on OrderID; OrderDate depends only on OrderID and transitive dependencies: CustomerName depends on non-key CustomerID.

(b) A designer for a hospital in Nairobi records these rules. A prescription can contain several drugs and a drug appears on many prescriptions. A patient may be admitted many times; each admission is for one patient. A ward holds many patients; an admitted patient is in one ward. (c) A music-streaming service in Seoul stores Artists, Albums, Tracks and Playlists. An artist releases many albums; an album has many tracks; a track can appear on many playlists and a playlist contains many tracks; each playlist is created by one user and a user can create many playlists. items.answer: (a) It models the entities and rules agreed with the client at a high level, so design errors (missing entities, wrong cardinalities) are found cheaply before implementation; it also communicates the design to non-technical stakeholders. (b) 6 tables: Drug, Prescription, Patient, Admission, Ward plus link table(s) DrugPrescription. (c) Entities: Artist, Album, Track, Playlist, User, PlaylistTrack (link). Artist 1:M Album; Album 1:M Track; User 1:M Playlist; Track M:N Playlist resolved by PlaylistTrack. Tables: Artist(ArtistID PK, Name), Album(AlbumID PK, Title, ArtistID FK), Track(TrackID PK, Title, Duration, AlbumID FK), User(UserID PK, Name), Playlist(PlaylistID PK, Name, UserID FK), PlaylistTrack(PlaylistID FK, TrackID FK, Position; PK (PlaylistID, TrackID)).

items.stem:
Case study context: Pacific Ride, a ride-sharing start-up in Lima, matches drivers to passengers using location data, trains models to set prices and builds its back end from reusable classes.
(a) With the help of a specific example, explain why a fully normalised database may sometimes be deliberately denormalised. Refer to Pacific Ride in your answer. [2]
(b) Evaluate the claim that Databases should always be normalised to third normal form. Refer to Pacific Ride in your answer. [4]
items.answer: (a) Highly normalised designs need many joins, which can slow read-heavy reporting; storing some redundant data (e.g. in a data warehouse) speeds up queries at the cost of extra storage and controlled redundancy. (A specific, correct example that illustrates this is required for full marks.) (b) For transactional (OLTP) systems 3NF is the right default; for analytical or performance-critical read workloads controlled denormalisation can be justified.
items.markingKey: (a) [2 marks] Award marks for: Highly normalised designs need many joins, which can slow read-heavy reporting; storing some redundant data (e.g. in a data warehouse) speeds up queries at the cost of extra storage and controlled redundancy. (A specific, correct example that illustrates this is required for full marks.) (one for each linked point in the chain of reasoning; no marks for assertion without explanation.) (b) [4 marks] Arguments for: removes redundancy and update/insert/delete anomalies; keeps data consistent and saves storage. Arguments against: more tables mean more joins, slowing read-heavy queries; data warehouses and analytics deliberately denormalise; design effort and complexity increase. Supported judgement: For transactional (OLTP) systems 3NF is the right default; for analytical or performance-critical read workloads controlled denormalisation can be justified. items.stem: "Validation in the application is sufficient; database constraints are unnecessary." Discuss.
items.answer: Both layers are needed: UI validation for usability and DBMS constraints as the final guarantee of integrity.
items.markingKey: Arguments for: application checks give immediate user feedback; fewer schema changes are needed. Arguments against: other applications, scripts and imports bypass application checks; constraints are enforced centrally and consistently; they document the rules in the schema. items.stem: "A three-level schema architecture adds unnecessary complexity for small projects." To what extent do you agree with this statement?
items.answer: Even small projects benefit from at least a clear logical design and views; the full formality can be scaled to the project size.
items.markingKey: Arguments for: small teams may design and implement in one step; fewer documents to maintain. Arguments against: data independence still makes later changes cheaper; views give security by restricting access; separating levels clarifies design decisions.
